newsitem.title: USA: EU meat negotiator heads home, blasts U.S. action.
newsitem.headline: EU meat negotiator heads home, blasts U.S. action.

text.p: The senior Euopean Union negotiator in recently failed talks with U.S. officials on meat inspection sharply criticised U.S. moves to curtail meat imports from Europe shortly before heading back to Brussels on Wednesday.

Briefing reporters one day after Washington and Brussels took separate actions that will halt hundreds of millions of dollars worth of meat and poultry trade, Lars Hoelgaard said that despite the stand-off, he hopes talks can be restarted soon.

He said he would contact Agriculture Department officials before he returned to Europe later in the day and may discuss dates to meet again, but that so far no further negotiations had been scheduled.
Hoelgaard stressed, however, that the U.S. move to require European meat and poultry packing plants to meet U.S. requirements was "totally unjustified" and will only make future talks more difficult.
"This will not impress us," said Hoelgaard. "We're not going to just sit back and let the U.S. take these kinds of actions."
Hoelgaard would not comment on what the EU's next move may be, but said taking the issue to the World Trade Organisation is "certainly a possibility."
A European Commission spokesman said earlier in Brussels that the EU has no plans to escalate the trade war, at least for the moment.

Hoelgaard denied charges by Washington that Europe's real agenda in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks has been to keep U.S. products out of Europe. "We're here to protect our health standards, not protect our trade," he said.
"We have been negotiating in good faith ... We have bent over backwards to accomodate the United States," Hoelgaard insisted.
Agreement on the issue would allow each side to accept meat and poultry products from the other even if inspection methods differ.

Hoelgaard said that significant progress had been made in the last round of talks, and that only a few issues remained unresolved -- specifically the issues of poultry decontamination and chilling, and "some red meat matters."

Washington has long complained that although the United States recognises equivalent meat inspection systems in Europe and has allowed European meat imports, Europe has insisted that U.S. plants conform to EU standards and has not been practicing equivalency.
Hoelgaard maintained that equivalency does not mean just agreeing on end-product specifications, but agreeing on specific steps to achieve the final result.
The U.S. meat and poultry industry had urged tough action if no agreement was reached in the talks, and industry officials widely applauded Washington's move on Tuesday.

Hoelgaard also said the U.S. action was "totally out of proportion." He noted that new EU regulations on poultry and dairy imports will impact some $75 million worth of U.S. shipments, while the Agriculture Department's new rules will halt around $300 million worth of EU products.
